claim: Working memory provides flexible storage of information in service of upcoming behavioral goals.
source: Working memory provides flexible storage of information in service of upcoming behavioral goals.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents a general theoretical position in the field.

claim: Some models propose specific fixed loci and mechanisms for the storage of visual information in working memory, such as sustained spiking in parietal and prefrontal cortex during working memory maintenance.
source: Some models propose specific fixed loci and mechanisms for the storage of visual information in working memory, such as sustained spiking in parietal and prefrontal cortex during working memory maintenance.
evidence: This statement references existing theoretical models in the literature.

claim: Information can be remembered in a flexible format that best suits current behavioral goals.
source: An alternative view is that information can be remembered in a flexible format that best suits current behavioral goals.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim representing an alternative hypothesis.

claim: Remembered visual information might be stored in sensory areas for easier comparison to future sensory inputs.
source: For example, remembered visual information might be stored in sensory areas for easier comparison to future sensory inputs, or might be re-coded into a more abstract action-oriented format and stored in motor areas.
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility presented as a hypothesis.

claim: Remembered visual information might be re-coded into a more abstract action-oriented format and stored in motor areas.
source: For example, remembered visual information might be stored in sensory areas for easier comparison to future sensory inputs, or might be re-coded into a more abstract action-oriented format and stored in motor areas.
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility presented as a hypothesis.

claim: There was less information about remembered spatial position in early visual and parietal regions when the required response was known versus unknown.
source: Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivariate decoding, we found that there was less information about remembered spatial position in early visual and parietal regions when the required response was known versus unknown.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's fMRI and decoding analyses.

claim: A representation of the planned motor action emerged in primary somatosensory, primary motor, and premotor cortex during the same task condition where spatial information was reduced in early visual cortex.
source: Furthermore, a representation of the planned motor action emerged in primary somatosensory, primary motor, and premotor cortex during the same task condition where spatial information was reduced in early visual cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's fMRI and decoding analyses.

claim: The neural networks supporting working memory can be strategically reconfigured depending on specific behavioral requirements during a canonical visual working memory paradigm.
source: These results suggest that the neural networks supporting working memory can be strategically reconfigured depending on specific behavioral requirements during a canonical visual working memory paradigm.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Working memory is thought to provide a flexible mental workspace which allows organisms to hold information in mind about past experiences and use it to guide future behavior.
source: Working memory (WM) is thought to provide a flexible mental workspace which allows organisms to hold information in mind about past experiences and use it to guide future behavior (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968; Baddeley and Hitch, 1974; Jonides et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational work in the field.

claim: The neural mechanisms of working memory are not universal across all tasks, but adaptively adjust to the requirements of the current situation.
source: Due to these varied demands, it is likely that the neural mechanisms of WM are not universal across all tasks, but adaptively adjust to the requirements of the current situation.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on logical inference from task variability.

claim: Most fMRI studies of visual working memory require participants to remember precise values of continuously varying features and to report these remembered features using responses that cannot be pre-planned during the delay period.
source: In most fMRI studies of visual WM, participants are required to remember precise values of continuously varying features, and to report these remembered features using responses that cannot be pre-planned during the delay period (Albers et al., 2013; Christophel et al., 2012; Ester et al., 2009; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Lorenc et al., 2018; Rademaker et al., 2019; Serences et al., 2009; Xing et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Tasks requiring memory for precise continuously varying features may encourage top-down recruitment of the same early sensory areas that support high-precision perceptual representations.
source: Such tasks may encourage top-down recruitment of the same early sensory areas that support high-precision perceptual representations (Awh and Jonides, 2001; Gazzaley and Nobre, 2012; Pasternak and Greenlee, 2005; Serences, 2016; Sreenivasan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most studies find that patterns of voxel activation measured in visual cortex encode information about specific feature values held in memory.
source: Consistent with this idea of sensory recruitment, most studies find that patterns of voxel activation measured in visual cortex encode information about specific feature values held in memory, supporting the role of visual cortex in maintaining detailed visual representations during WM.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from multiple prior studies.

claim: Single unit recordings made during memory-guided saccade tasks suggest an important role for the prefrontal cortex in maintaining remembered information across brief delay periods.
source: Single unit recordings made during these tasks suggest an important role for the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in maintaining remembered information across brief delay periods (Funahashi et al., 1989; Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Goldman-Rakic, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to electrophysiology studies.

claim: Action-oriented working memory may rely more heavily on areas involved in planning and motor production, and less on early sensory cortex.
source: Consistent with these findings, others have suggested that action-oriented WM in general may rely more heavily on areas involved in planning and motor production, and less on early sensory cortex (Boettcher et al., 2021; Curtis et al., 2004; Myers et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Information related to the same stimulus might be stored at several different loci and in different formats.
source: Consistent with this idea, there are indications that even information related to the same stimulus might be stored at several different loci and in different formats (Iamshchinina et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2013; Rademaker et al., 2019; Serences, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An alternative theory of working memory storage suggests that memory-related signals in early sensory areas are epiphenomenal.
source: Indeed, an alternative theory of WM storage suggests that memory-related signals in early sensory areas are epiphenomenal, in which case, task goals are not expected to affect the strength of representations in this part of the brain (Leavitt et al., 2017; Xu, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Participants were significantly faster in the informative condition compared to the uninformative condition.
source: Participants were significantly faster in the informative condition (informative mean ± SEM: 0.57 ± 0.03 s; uninformative: 1.08 ± 0.06 s; t(5) = –9.618; p<0.001)
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the main task, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Participants were more accurate in the informative condition compared to the uninformative condition.
source: and also more accurate in the informative condition (informative mean ± SEM: 93.92 ± 2.12%; uninformative: 89.83 ± 1.12%; t(5)=3.463; p=0.018).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the main task, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The behavioral benefits suggest that participants used the preview disk to pre-plan their motor action in the informative condition.
source: These behavioral benefits suggest that participants used the preview disk to pre-plan their motor action in the informative condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing faster and more accurate responses.

claim: The BOLD signal in all retinotopic ROIs increased following visual stimulation.
source: As expected, the BOLD signal in all retinotopic ROIs increased following visual stimulation (Figure 1D, left two panels; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a univariate fMRI result shown in the figures.

claim: Occipital retinotopic areas V1–hV4 do not show sustained BOLD activation during the memory delay period in either task condition.
source: We also replicated the typical finding that occipital retinotopic areas V1–hV4 do not show sustained BOLD activation during the memory delay period (Offen et al., 2009; Riggall and Postle, 2012; Serences et al., 2009; Harrison and Tong, 2009) in either of our two task conditions.
evidence: This is a univariate fMRI result that replicates prior findings.

claim: Mean BOLD responses in parietal areas IPS0-3 showed elevated late delay period activation in the uninformative condition relative to the informative condition.
source: Also as expected, mean BOLD responses in parietal areas IPS0-3 showed elevated late delay period activation in the uninformative condition relative to the informative condition.
evidence: This is a univariate fMRI result shown in the figures.

claim: Sensorimotor areas S1, M1, and PMc showed higher mean BOLD responses in the informative compared with the uninformative condition at several timepoints early in the delay period.
source: Sensorimotor areas S1, M1, and PMc showed a condition difference in the opposite direction, with higher mean BOLD responses in the informative compared with the uninformative condition at several timepoints early in the delay period, consistent with an increased reliance on an action-oriented memory code (Calderon et al., 2018; Donner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a univariate fMRI result shown in the figures, with interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Reliable interhemispheric differences can be observed in sensorimotor areas, with higher activation in the hemisphere contralateral to the planned button press in the informative condition.
source: As expected, reliable interhemispheric differences can also be observed in sensorimotor areas, with higher activation in the hemisphere contralateral to the planned button press in the informative condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a univariate fMRI result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spatial decoding accuracy was strongest in early visual areas V1, V2, V3, and V3AB, and became progressively weaker at more anterior regions of the visual hierarchy.
source: The results of this multivariate analysis demonstrate that across the uninformative and the informative conditions, spatial decoding accuracy was strongest in early visual areas V1, V2, V3, and V3AB, and became progressively weaker at more anterior regions of the visual hierarchy (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a multivariate decoding result shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spatial decoding accuracy was at chance in the three sensorimotor areas S1, M1, and PMc.
source: Spatial decoding accuracy was at chance in the three sensorimotor areas S1, M1, and PMc.
evidence: This is a multivariate decoding result shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Decoding accuracy in most retinotopic areas was significantly higher for the uninformative condition compared to the informative condition.
source: Importantly, there was also a pronounced effect of task condition (Figure 2B and C). Decoding accuracy in most retinotopic areas was significantly higher for the uninformative condition, in which participants were forced to rely on a spatial memory code, compared to the informative condition, in which participants could convert to an action-oriented memory for the button press required at the end of the delay (two-way repeated measures ANOVA with ROI and task condition as factors: main effect of ROI: F(13,65) = 24.548, p<0.001; main effect of task condition: F(1,5) = 35.537, p=0.001; ROI × condition interaction F(13,65) = 5.757, p<0.001; p-values obtained using permutation test; see Methods, Analysis: Spatial position decoding).
evidence: This is a multivariate decoding result with statistical testing shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Spatial decoding accuracy was significantly higher in the uninformative compared to the informative condition in V1–hV4, LO2, and IPS0.
source: Pairwise comparisons showed that spatial decoding accuracy was significantly higher in the uninformative compared to the informative condition in V1–hV4, LO2, and IPS0.
evidence: This is a multivariate decoding result with pairwise statistical comparisons shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In later IPS subregions (IPS1-3), spatial decoding accuracy was above chance in the uninformative memory condition, but at chance in the informative condition, without a significant difference between conditions.
source: In later IPS subregions (IPS1-3), spatial decoding accuracy was above chance in the uninformative memory condition, but at chance in the informative condition, without a significant difference between conditions.
evidence: This is a multivariate decoding result shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The difference in spatial decoding accuracy between conditions was not present during and immediately after encoding of the target dot, when the trial condition was not yet known.
source: Finally, time-resolved analyses revealed that this difference between the conditions was not present during and immediately after encoding of the target dot, when the trial condition was not yet known.
evidence: This is a time-resolved multivariate decoding result shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Condition differences in spatial decoding emerged approximately 5–6 s after the presentation of the preview disk and persisted until the final response disk appeared.
source: Instead, condition differences emerged approximately 5–6 s after the presentation of the preview disk and persisted until the final response disk appeared (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a time-resolved multivariate decoding result shown in the figures.

claim: The difference in spatial decoding accuracy between task conditions replicated when training and testing a decoder using data from within each condition of the main working memory task.
source: Importantly, the difference in spatial decoding accuracy between task conditions replicated when we trained and tested a decoder using data from within each condition of the main WM task as opposed to training on the independent spatial WM task. This indicates that the difference between task conditions was robust to a range of analysis choices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; see Methods, Analysis: Spatial position decoding).
evidence: This is a multivariate decoding result using a different analysis approach shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The orientation of the preview disk could be decoded with above chance accuracy in several visual cortex ROIs in both conditions, but without a significant difference between conditions.
source: A supplementary analysis revealed that the orientation of the preview disk (i.e. the boundary between its light- and dark-gray sides) could be decoded with above chance accuracy in several visual cortex ROIs in both conditions, but without a significant difference between conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; see Methods, Analysis: Preview disk orientation decoding for details).
evidence: This is a multivariate decoding result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neural processing of the preview disk was not modulated by task condition.
source: This indicates that neural processing of the preview disk, a visual stimulus physically presented on the screen, was not modulated by task condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preview disk decoding analysis.

claim: The effect of task condition on information content was specific to the spatial memory representation itself, and not due to a more global modulatory effect or difference in the signal-to-noise ratio of representations in early visual cortex.
source: Therefore, the effect of task condition on information content was specific to the spatial memory representation itself, and not due to a more global modulatory effect or difference in the signal-to-noise ratio of representations in early visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preview disk decoding analysis.

claim: Above chance decoding of upcoming actions was found in each of the three sensorimotor ROIs (S1, M1, and PMc) in the informative condition but not the uninformative condition.
source: This analysis revealed above chance decoding of upcoming actions in each of the three sensorimotor ROIs (S1, M1, and PMc) in the informative condition but not the uninformative condition.
evidence: This is a multivariate action decoding result shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All retinotopic visual ROIs showed chance level action decoding for both conditions.
source: In contrast, all retinotopic visual ROIs showed chance level action decoding for both conditions (two-way repeated measures ANOVA with ROI and task condition as factors: main effect of ROI: F(13,65) = 4.003, p<0.001; main effect of condition F(1,5) = 3.802, p=0.106; ROI × condition interaction: F(13,65) = 2.937, p=0.001; p-values obtained using permutation test; see Methods, Analysis: Action decoding).
evidence: This is a multivariate action decoding result with statistical testing shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the informative condition, information about a participants' upcoming action began to emerge approximately 4 s after the onset of the preview disk stimulus.
source: A time-resolved decoding analysis revealed that, in the informative condition, information about a participants' upcoming action began to emerge approximately 4 s after the onset of the preview disk stimulus, decreased slightly toward the end of the delay period, then rose steeply after the response disk onset when the participant actually executed a motor action (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a time-resolved multivariate action decoding result shown in the figures.

claim: The increase in action decoding accuracy during the last part of the trial appeared sooner for the informative condition than the uninformative condition.
source: The increase in action decoding accuracy during the last part of the trial appeared sooner for the informative condition than the uninformative condition, in agreement with the speeding of behavioral response times in the informative condition (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a time-resolved multivariate action decoding result shown in Figure 3B, with reference to behavioral data in Figure 1B.

claim: Spatial position information generalized from sensory-driven perceptual training data to both conditions of the main working memory task.
source: We found that spatial position information generalized from this sensory-driven perceptual training data to both conditions of our main WM task (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a cross-generalization decoding result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The coding format used during spatial working memory is sensory-like in nature, closely resembling the responses in visual cortex to spatially localized perceptual input.
source: This result supports the idea that the coding format used during spatial WM is sensory-like in nature, closely resembling the responses in visual cortex to spatially localized perceptual input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-generalization decoding result from Figure 4A.

claim: Decoding performance in early visual and parietal areas was higher for the uninformative than the informative condition when training on sensory-driven perceptual data.
source: Importantly, decoding performance in early visual and parietal areas was again higher for the uninformative than the informative condition.
evidence: This is a cross-generalization decoding result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The uninformative condition of the task resulted in a stronger and more 'sensory-like' memory code.
source: This implies that the uninformative condition of our task resulted in a stronger and more 'sensory-like' memory code.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-generalization decoding result from Figure 4A.

claim: Above-chance decoding accuracy of the participant's upcoming action was found in S1, M1, and PMc in the informative condition only when training on data from a button-pressing task.
source: This analysis revealed above-chance decoding accuracy of the participant's upcoming action in S1, M1, and PMc, in the informative condition only (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a cross-generalization decoding result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The memory representations in the informative condition were stored in a more motor-like format which closely resembled signals measured during actual button press responses.
source: This result supports the idea that the memory representations in the informative condition were stored in a more motor-like format which closely resembled signals measured during actual button press responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-generalization decoding result from Figure 4B.

claim: Task requirements are a critical determinant of how and where working memory is implemented in the brain.
source: Here we demonstrate, within a single spatial WM paradigm, that task requirements are a critical determinant of how and where WM is implemented in the brain.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Working memory flexibly engages different cortical areas and coding formats, even in the context of a task that is commonly used to study a single underlying construct (i.e. visuo-spatial working memory).
source: More importantly, however, our data show that WM flexibly engages different cortical areas and coding formats, even in the context of a task that is commonly used to study a single underlying construct (i.e. visuo-spatial WM).
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The brain's mechanisms for storage are not fully specified by the type of information being remembered, but instead depend on how the encoded information will be used to guide future behavior.
source: These findings highlight the goal-oriented nature of WM: the brain's mechanisms for storage are not fully specified by the type of information being remembered, but instead depend on how the encoded information will be used to guide future behavior.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Visual areas V1–hV4 and LO2 showed no sustained BOLD responses or differences in the mean BOLD signal between conditions during the delay period, despite these areas showing condition differences in spatial decoding accuracy.
source: Specifically, visual areas V1–hV4 and LO2 showed no sustained BOLD responses or differences in the mean BOLD signal between conditions during the delay period, despite these areas showing condition differences in spatial decoding accuracy.
evidence: This is a comparison of univariate and multivariate results shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2.

claim: The observed differences in decoding performance cannot be explained by global changes in signal due to arousal or task difficulty, but are instead attributable to differences in the amount of information represented within population-level patterns of activation in visual cortex.
source: It additionally suggests that the observed differences in decoding performance cannot be explained by global changes in signal due to arousal or task difficulty, but are instead attributable to differences in the amount of information represented within population-level patterns of activation in visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dissociation between univariate and multivariate results.

claim: Information about the preview disk was not significantly different between task conditions.
source: Furthermore, we found that information about the preview disk (see Figure 1A), a physical stimulus that appeared briefly on the screen early in the delay period, was not significantly different between task conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a multivariate decoding result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The observed modulation of spatial decoding accuracy in visual cortex was specific to the memory representation, and not due to a non-specific change in signal-to-noise ratio within early visual areas.
source: This finding further highlights that the observed modulation of spatial decoding accuracy in visual cortex was specific to the memory representation, and not due to a non-specific change in signal-to-noise ratio within early visual areas.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preview disk decoding analysis.

claim: In multiple subregions of IPS, higher univariate delay period activation was observed for the uninformative condition relative to the informative condition.
source: At the same time, in multiple subregions of IPS, we did observe higher univariate delay period activation for the uninformative condition relative to the informative condition.
evidence: This is a univariate fMRI result shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In sensorimotor areas, the opposite pattern was observed with higher activation in the informative condition.
source: In contrast, the opposite was true in sensorimotor areas (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a univariate fMRI result shown in the figures.

claim: With the possible exception of area V1, decoding accuracy did not fall entirely to chance in early visual cortex during informative cue trials, even at the very end of the working memory delay period.
source: While information about the remembered spatial position was substantially lower in the informative condition than the uninformative condition, decoding accuracy did not fall entirely to chance in early visual cortex during informative cue trials (Figure 2B). With the possible exception of area V1, this was true even when looking at decoding at the very end of the WM delay period (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a multivariate decoding result shown in the figures.

claim: It is possible that on some fraction of informative trials, participants failed to properly encode or process the condition cue, and as a result maintained a high-precision spatial representation throughout the delay period.
source: First, it is possible that on some fraction of informative trials, participants failed to properly encode or process the condition cue, and as a result maintained a high-precision spatial representation throughout the delay period.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for above-chance decoding in the informative condition.

claim: It is possible that participants faithfully followed the informative cue and made use of an action-oriented strategy, but some amount of visuo-spatial memory information was nonetheless maintained in visual cortex.
source: Second, it is possible that participants faithfully followed the informative cue, and made use of an action-oriented strategy, but some amount of visuo-spatial memory information was nonetheless maintained in visual cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for above-chance decoding in the informative condition.

claim: The recruitment of sensory-like codes in visual cortex is at least partially obligatory when performing a visuo-spatial working memory task.
source: This would suggest that the recruitment of sensory-like codes in visual cortex is at least partially obligatory when performing a visuo-spatial WM task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the above-chance decoding in the informative condition.

claim: Information about upcoming actions became detectable around 4 s after the onset of the preview disk.
source: In our data, information regarding the upcoming action became detectable around 4 s after the onset of the preview disk – roughly the same time that spatial decoding accuracy in visual cortex dropped in the informative compared to the uninformative condition (Figure 2C and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a time-resolved multivariate decoding result shown in the figures.

claim: Information about upcoming actions declined toward the end of the delay period, dropping to chance just before the response disk appeared.
source: Additionally, we found that information about upcoming actions declined toward the end of the delay period, dropping to chance just before the response disk appeared (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a time-resolved multivariate decoding result shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The time course of action information is consistent with a transient signal related to the initial formation of an action-oriented memory representation.
source: This time course is consistent with a transient signal related to the initial formation of an action-oriented memory representation, and aligns with recent EEG findings in human motor cortex following a retro-cue in a visual WM task (Boettcher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the time-resolved action decoding result, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: High priority items tend to be represented more robustly than items that are not immediately relevant to behavior.
source: For instance, it has been shown that high priority items, meaning those that are relevant for upcoming actions, tend to be represented more robustly than items that are not immediately relevant to behavior (Christophel et al., 2012; Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012; Lorenc et al., 2020; Rose et al., 2016; Sprague et al., 2016; but see also Barbosa et al., 2021; Iamshchinina et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Prioritized working memory representations can be reconfigured so that they are optimized for future behavior, which may include the activation of circuits related to motor output.
source: Prioritized WM representations can be further reconfigured so that they are optimized for future behavior, which may include the activation of circuits related to motor output (Myers et al., 2017; Nobre and Stokes, 2019; Schneider et al., 2017; Souza and Oberauer, 2016; van Ede et al., 2019a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When retrieving or selecting an item within working memory, eye movements exhibit a systematic bias toward the spatial position at which the item was originally presented, even without a physical stimulus to guide eye movements.
source: For instance, prior work has demonstrated that when retrieving or selecting an item within WM, eye movements exhibit a systematic bias toward the spatial position at which the item was originally presented, even without a physical stimulus to guide eye movements (Spivey and Geng, 2001; Ferreira et al., 2008; van Ede et al., 2019b; van Ede et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Eye movements may play a functional role in retrieving items from working memory.
source: These eye movements may play a functional role in retrieving items from WM (Ferreira et al., 2008; van Ede et al., 2019b) and can index processes such as attentional selection within WM (van Ede et al., 2019b; van Ede et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When participants make a saccade during the delay period of a visual working memory task, memory performance is enhanced for items originally presented at the saccade target location.
source: For example, when participants make a saccade during the delay period of a visual WM task, memory performance is enhanced for items originally presented at the saccade target location (Ohl and Rolfs, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The planning of both memory-guided saccades and anti-saccades is associated with topographically specific activation in early visual cortex measured with fMRI.
source: Finally, the planning of both memory-guided saccades and anti-saccades is associated with topographically specific activation in early visual cortex measured with fMRI, suggesting that neural representations of upcoming actions are coded similarly to representations used for WM storage (Saber et al., 2015; Rahmati et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Instructing participants to maintain items in a visual, verbal, or semantic code resulted in format-specific patterns of neural activation measured with fMRI.
source: Similarly, another experiment showed that instructing participants to maintain items in a visual, verbal, or semantic code resulted in format-specific patterns of neural activation measured with fMRI (Lewis-Peacock et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Participants were explicitly instructed to withhold any physical finger movements or button presses until the end of the delay period, when the probe disk appeared.
source: This interpretation is justified because participants were explicitly instructed to withhold any physical finger movements or button presses until the end of the delay period, when the probe disk appeared.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The BOLD response is driven in part by modulations of local field potentials.
source: For example, the BOLD response is driven in part by modulations of local field potentials (Boynton, 2011; Goense and Logothetis, 2008; Logothetis et al., 2001; Logothetis and Wandell, 2004), which may contain information about remembered features, such as motion direction, even when single unit spike rates do not (Mendoza-Halliday et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some non-human primate studies use tasks that allow for motor coding strategies, such as the traditional memory-guided saccade paradigm.
source: For example, some NHP studies use tasks that allow for motor coding strategies, such as the traditional memory-guided saccade paradigm (Funahashi et al., 1989; Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Goldman-Rakic, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Non-human primate tasks often require animals to remember one of a small, discrete set of stimuli.
source: Another aspect of task design that may contribute to these differences is that NHP tasks often require animals to remember one of a small, discrete set of stimuli (e.g. Funahashi et al., 1993; Mendoza-Halliday et al., 2014; Miller et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some non-human primate electrophysiology studies have shown spiking activity in V1 that reflects the contents of working memory using tasks that require precise spatial representations.
source: For example, some NHP electrophysiology studies have shown spiking activity in V1 that reflects the contents of WM using tasks that require precise spatial representations that may not be easily re-coded into a non-sensory format (e.g. the curve-tracing task used by Van Kerkoerle and colleagues; Supèr et al., 2001; van Kerkoerle et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When participants were given the possibility to switch from a purely visual to a motor-based working memory code, the amount of information regarding precise spatial position dropped in early visual and parietal cortex.
source: When our participants were given the possibility to switch from a purely visual to a motor-based WM code, the amount of information regarding precise spatial position dropped in early visual and parietal cortex, while information about an upcoming action became decodable from sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: When participants were given the possibility to switch from a purely visual to a motor-based working memory code, information about an upcoming action became decodable from sensorimotor cortex.
source: When our participants were given the possibility to switch from a purely visual to a motor-based WM code, the amount of information regarding precise spatial position dropped in early visual and parietal cortex, while information about an upcoming action became decodable from sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: Six participants between the ages of 20 and 34 were recruited from the University of California, San Diego community.
source: Six participants (two male) between the ages of 20 and 34 were recruited from the University of California, San Diego (UCSD) community (mean age 27.2 ± 2.7 years).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at UCSD.
source: The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at UCSD, and all participants provided written informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent.
source: The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at UCSD, and all participants provided written informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: All MRI scanning was performed on a General Electric Discovery MR750 3.0T research-dedicated scanner at the UC San Diego Keck Center for Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
source: All MRI scanning was performed on a General Electric (GE) Discovery MR750 3.0T research-dedicated scanner at the UC San Diego Keck Center for Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
evidence: This is a description of the MRI equipment and procedures.

claim: Functional echo-planar imaging data were acquired using a Nova Medical 32-channel head coil and the Stanford Simultaneous Multislice EPI sequence.
source: Functional echo-planar imaging (EPI) data were acquired using a Nova Medical 32-channel head coil (NMSC075-32-3GE-MR750) and the Stanford Simultaneous Multislice (SMS) EPI sequence (MUX EPI), with a multiband factor of 8 and 9 axial slices per band (total slices = 72; 2 mm3 isotropic; 0 mm gap; matrix = 104 × 104; field of view (FOV) = 20.8 cm; repetition time/time to echo (TR/TE) = 800/35 ms; flip angle = 52°; inplane acceleration = 1).
evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition parameters.
